reason: The sources support a compelling 45-second story backed by 15 fully verified claims with citations across independent sites.
story: On September 1, 1859, astronomer Richard Carrington witnessed two blinding white flashes on the Sun. Less than eighteen hours later, a massive coronal mass ejection slammed into Earth's magnetic field, triggering the largest geomagnetic storm in recorded history. Typically, solar eruptions take several days to reach Earth, but an earlier blast had cleared the path. The resulting auroras were so bright that people in the northeastern U.S. could read newspapers at midnight, and Rocky Mountain gold miners woke up to cook breakfast thinking dawn had arrived. The skies glowed blood-red as far south as Cuba and Hawaii. Across North America and Europe, induced electric currents caused telegraph lines to spark, shock operators, and catch fire. In an astonishing twist, telegraph operators in Boston and Portland unplugged their batteries completely and transmitted messages for two hours powered solely by the magnetic storm itself.
angle: Telegraph operators in 1859 unplugged their batteries and successfully sent messages for two hours using only the electric current induced by a solar storm.

claims.claim: On September 1, 1859, English astronomer Richard Carrington observed a powerful solar flare on the Sun.
Astronomer Richard Hodgson independently observed the solar flare on September 1, 1859.
The white-light solar flare observed by Carrington lasted for about five minutes.
The coronal mass ejection traveled approximately 150 million kilometers (90 million miles) to Earth in only 17.6 hours.
Typical coronal mass ejections take three to four days to travel from the Sun to Earth.
The Carrington CME traveled unusually fast because a prior CME had cleared out ambient solar wind plasma.
The geomagnetic storm produced auroras bright enough for people in the northeastern United States to read newspapers at night.
Gold miners in the Rocky Mountains woke up and began preparing breakfast because the bright aurora made them think morning had arrived.
Auroras during the event expanded far equatorward, becoming visible in low-latitude locations including Cuba and Hawaii.
Geomagnetically induced currents caused telegraph systems across Europe and North America to fail, throw sparks, and set fires.
Telegraph operators received electric shocks from their equipment due to the induced currents.
Telegraph operators on the line between Boston and Portland disconnected their batteries and communicated for about two hours using only the induced auroral current.
A similar Carrington-class solar superstorm erupted in July 2012 but narrowly missed Earth.
The July 2012 solar superstorm directly struck NASA's STEREO-A spacecraft, which safely recorded detailed data.
Studies estimate a modern Carrington-level solar storm hitting Earth could cause trillions of dollars in damage to the U.S. economy.

disputed: Nitrate spikes in ice cores: Early claims attributed nitrate spikes in Greenland ice cores to the Carrington Event, but subsequent research indicates these spikes correlate with terrestrial forest fires rather than solar proton events (leave out or attribute).
Geomagnetic storm Dst values: Estimates of the peak Dst index range from -800 nT to -1750 nT (-0.80 to -1.75 μT) due to off-scale readings on 19th-century magnetometers (attribute range).
Bombay magnetometer interpretation: Researchers debate whether the Bombay magnetometer recorded ring current intensity or nearby auroral electrojet magnetic field perturbations (leave out).
